subtopic: TRAINING OF UNITED KINGDOM UNITS IN CANADA

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minisler of National Defence):
subtopic: TRAINING OF UNITED KINGDOM UNITS IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement with regard to the training of British army units in Canada during the forthcoming months. The house will recall that last summer, in response to a request from the United Kingdom government, the Canadian government agreed to a battalion of the British army being airlifted to Camp Gagetown in June to train with the 3rd Canadian brigade group. This exercise proved of value to all concerned.
This year, and again at the request of the United Kingdom government, we have agreed to a battalion joining Canadian regular army forces in Canada for summer training. The first battalion of the Royal Welsh Fusiliers has been nominated. Details as to the location of the training area are now being worked out and will be announced in due course. As was the case last year, the United Kingdom will bear the total administrative costs. In addition, the Canadian government has also agreed to a proposal that a British army battery and a parachute company should come to Canada later this year and early in 1963 to obtain training experience under winter conditions.
I am sure all hon. members will appreciate this further evidence of the close co-operation which exists between Canada and the United Kingdom in matters relating to our common defence effort.

ACTS OF TERRORISM, B.C.    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to move the adjournment of the house, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay East, under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the need for federal assistance to the provincial government of British Columbia to effectively deal with the extremely serious situation in the Kootenays caused by continuous bombings and acts of terrorism, culminating two days ago in the destruction of half a million dollars worth of property causing unemployment to over 1,000 persons for a period of a few weeks to months.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ACTS OF TERRORISM, B.C.    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Before I hear the minister, perhaps I should ask the hon. member who requests leave to indicate, if he can, what is the urgency of debate. The problem of bombings and other unlawful acts by certain people in the Kootenays has engaged the attention of this house and of the country for a long time. It is true that there was recently an outbreak with particularly serious consequences to which the hon. member has referred. However, I wonder whether or not that creates an urgency of debate in a continuing problem. I would ask the hon. member to address himself briefly to that point, then I shall hear from the Minister of Justice.

subtopic: ACTS OF TERRORISM, B.C.    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ACTS OF TERRORISM, B.C.    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: The question is urgency of debate. Recognizing that there is a serious problem, it is a continuing one. Is there some new aspect to it now which it has not been possible to debate in this session or will not be possible to debate within a reasonable time?

subtopic: ACTS OF TERRORISM, B.C.    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The urgency of the situation for the people of the Kootenays is in the fact that according to some it has now almost reached the stage of civil war with these continued bombings, acts of terrorism and sabotage. The mayors of the various cities in the Kootenays, the heads of industrial organizations and numerous unions have wired members of the government, including the

Acts of Terrorism in B.C.
Prime Minister, the member for Kootenay West and the member for Kootenay East, urging the federal government to take action. They believe the urgency is very particular at the present time, and it is on that basis I moved the adjournment of the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ACTS OF TERRORISM, B.C.    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
If I may say a word on this, I would prefer not to deal directly with the question of urgency because, as a minister coming from British Columbia, you will appreciate that I am aware of the nature of the problem and the serious aspect it has taken on just lately. Whether or not that kind of urgency brings it within the rule regarding urgency of debate is a question Your Honour has raised which I am content to leave where, I submit with respect and deference, you have correctly summarized it.
There are two other grounds on which I think the motion is out of order, and it is with those I should like to deal. The first is based on citation 100 in Beauchesne's fourth edition, page 89, where he says:
The definite matter of urgent public importance for the discussion of which a member may ask leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 must involve the administrative responsibility of the government.
The constitutional position, sir, as is well known, is that the responsibility for the maintenance of law and order and the protection of property is that of the provinces. So long, therefore, as the province accepts this responsibility there is no way that the federal government can intervene to give assistance in this field, so there is at present no way in which any question of the administrative responsibility of the federal government arises. No indication has been received that the province of British Columbia does not accept the responsibility of maintaining law and order. Therefore, as I say, there is no way in which this matter could come within the administrative responsibility of the federal government.
In saying this, I would not want to be taken as implying that responsibility would automatically be accepted if a request were made. There are relevant statutes and other provisions in this regard with respect to the kind of assistance and the circumstances under which assistance of the kind referred-that is, military aid and extra policing-can be requested by a province. These would have to be looked at, and certainly would be looked at, at once to see whether or not these circumstances prevailed if any such request were made. The point that is important to note here for the purpose which we are dealing with now is that no request has been made by the province. There is no indication that the province does not accept the responsibility


or feels it cannot discharge the responsibility for the maintenance of law and order. In those circumstances I submit that it is not a matter within the scope of the citation to which I have referred.
I repeat that I do not want to take what I may call, with respect, the narrow ground with regard to urgency, although I do submit with deference that you have correctly stated the position there. Rather I prefer to rest on the ground I have referred to, and on the ground contained in paragraph 5 of citation 100 at page 90 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, namely:
The adjournment of the house cannot be moved with reference to critical conditions generally prevailing in certain parts of the country.
Although it is British Columbia's misfortune, nevertheless fortunately the conditions prevailing in the constituency of my hon. friend from Kootenay West are not those generally prevailing across the country.
So on those two grounds, while respecting fully the desire of the hon. member for Kootenay West and the hon. member for Kootenay East and their anxiety in this matter, and while indicating that all hon. members in the house share that anxiety-certainly the government shares and understands their concern-nevertheless in my respectful submission this is not the kind of subject that can be debated here at this time, for the reasons I have given.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ACTS OF TERRORISM, B.C.    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I am not sure whether the hon. member who is asking for leave feels that the matter has been sufficiently placed before the attention of the government to allow his request to stand, or whether he would like me to deal with it on its merits.

subtopic: ACTS OF TERRORISM, B.C.    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I have listened to the minister's explanation with great interest, and in view of the facts he placed before the house I feel I have nothing further to say at this time.

speechtext:
I would like to ask a question of the Prime Minister in view of the forthcoming disarmament meeting at Geneva next week. Does the government consider that the first and essential step in reaching a general

disarmament agreement should be an agreement to end all nuclear tests, with appropriate provision for inspection and control, and that this should be given first priority at the forthcoming conference?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PRIORITY OF AGREEMENT ON NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext:
There is no doubt that the question of nuclear tests will be raised. There are to be preliminary discussions on that point among the foreign ministers of the United Kingdom, the United States and the Soviet union commencing on Monday, and there probably will be subsequent discussions in the disarmament committee itself. But I think it would be unwise for Canada to insist that this question of nuclear tests must be settled before the committee undertakes any discussion of the broader question of disarmament.
We shall be doing our best in the general field of disarmament to bring about an end to nuclear tests, but I do not think there should be a rigid dividing line between the discussions on these two subjects, such as the Leader of the Opposition would appear to be suggesting.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to participate in a debate on this item but, rather unusually, we have played a bit of hopscotch in connection with the items in these estimates.

speechtext: I have informed all parties.
Could all members of the committee be informed by the house leader as to the likely order in which the various departments will be taken up?

speechtext: Then the Department of Forestry, which was just about completed the other day, then citizenship and immigration, and after that we will carry on in the order in which they are in the further supplementary estimates.
Thank you.

Mr. Chairman, we have not had from the minister a report on the situation that prevails in the countries covered by the three international commissions for supervision and control, in South and North Viet Nam, Cambodia and Laos. The minister will recall that toward the close of the last session there was some discussion on his estimates about developments in Laos and particularly with regard to the reactivated international commission on which Canada, along with Poland and India, serves.
At that time the minister expressed an optimistic note. He said that notwithstanding difficulties that had prevailed from the month of January, 1961 up until the summer of 1961, he was confident that the situation in that particular section of old Indo-China would evolve in a manner that did not warrant some of the apprehensions that I and several other members affirmed. I am sure that on this item the minister will want to bring the house up to date as to the situation in Laos.
The position taken by the United States, the United Kingdom and the Soviet union,

along with lesser powers, was that there should be established in Laos a government that would be truly neutral in character. That seemed to be one of the ways, it was thought at the Geneva conference, by which stability and peace could be provided for this area. As we all know, however, notwithstanding the apparent agreement to establish a government under the former prime minister, notwithstanding the meeting of the three royal princes including the present prime minister of the government of Laos, the former prime minister, Souvanna Phouma, and the leader of the Pathet Lao, since last summer there has been no disposition by these three gentlemen to effect conditions which would have permitted the establishment of a truly neutral government, along lines envisaged by the United Kingdom and the United States.
I am not saying that it will be possible to establish a truly neutral government because of the incursions that have taken place in Laos by guerilla activity emanating from certain communist lands. Canada, however, has a very important stake in the outcome of events in Laos. The reactivation of the truce supervisory commission, which adjourned sine die over a year and a half ago, was effected to determine whether pursuant to agreement, there had been in fact a cease-fire between the Pathet Lao forces and those of the royal government. Since the beginning of the time Mr. Mayrand as our representative on that commission took over his functions in Delhi, prior to going to Laos, there have been skirmishes and conflicts between the opposing forces. It would be interesting to know what progress the commission has been able to make in determining in fact whether there has been a cease fire and whether in fact the commission has been able to fulfil the functions for which it was set up a second time.
It would also be of value to hear from the minister if the material shortage situation continues. When we discussed this matter last there was not provided to the commission, as I recall, necessary air equipment to enable the commission to discharge its functions effectively. These and other questions perhaps better known to the minister, will be of interest to the house and to the country. We would appreciate having from him a report with regard to the commission in Laos. What is to be its likely tenure? How effective has its work been?
I am not suggesting that it has not been effective, nor am I suggesting that the commission has not made every endeavour to make a useful contribution to the situation which prevails in an area adjacent to which are such nations as Cambodia, South Viet 26207-1-102
Supply-External Affairs Nam, Thailand, Burma and other countries in south and southeast Asia, all of which have a direct involvement. It would be interesting to know whether the minister believes that the evidence is that the Soviet union has made every endeavour to co-operate along the lines originally agreed on, and if the difficulties which have arisen come from another communist nation and not from the Soviet union.
Then, of course, on this item we would want to hear from the minister as to the situation with regard to the commission in Cambodia. There relative peace prevails but, as we know from earlier discussion, the obligations of the commission in that little country have not been great in the last four or five years. One could successfully argue, I think, that the commission there might well have been disbanded. However, there were good reasons, I believe, for continuing the commission, reasons essentially exemplary, because of the situation that attends the government of Laos and of South Viet Nam. I take it that although the commission continues to be in existence in Cambodia, there has been no successful resistance to the contention of Canada that it should not concern itself with boundary matters.
Then there is the third commission in South Viet Nam. In the last four or five months we have been hearing a good deal about South Viet Nam. We are told that this has become a very critical area, in which the United States, through its president and secretary of state, has indicated a deep concern and interest. It is a country into which are flowing military contributions, materiel and personnel, to assist directly or indirectly the government of President Diem against infiltrations and attacks originating within and more particularly from North Viet Nam.
Now, certainly when this commission and the other two commissions were established in 1954, as a result of the Geneva accord, it was not envisaged that the responsibilities of the three participating countries on the commission would have as extended a period of operation as has proved to be the case. I am sure we will agree with the minister's statement last summer, and with similar statements made by his predecessor earlier, that these three commissions have served an important and steadying purpose at the time they were established. They continued to provide a measure of stability and peace in all three countries. But it is a fact that in 1956 the situation had so developed in at least two countries, South Viet Nam and Cambodia, that there was some reason for Canada to anticipate that the period of the commission's usefulness was perhaps approaching an end, although in the case of Laos I believe

Supply-External Affairs the position of Canada, notwithstanding the wish of the royal government, was that the commission had not yet fulfilled its purpose.
Canada is represented on these commissions. It has a civilian representative in South Viet Nam, as in the two other countries. There are military personnel, I do not know to what extent, in all three countries. Perhaps the minister will inform us about this. In any event we have a considerable number of Canadians serving in the cause of mediation and the cause of peace in these three countries. It would be interesting, because of the continued and disturbing internal conflict which prevails in South Viet Nam in particular, to know what the attitude of the Canadian government is with regard to this situation, particularly with regard to the operations of the commission in South Viet Nam. It would be interesting to know the significance of the recent bombings of the palace in Saigon.
Many people suggest that the situation there is second only in importance, in so far as the peace of the world is concerned, to the situation in divided Germany. Whether that is the case, we are participating in the commission in South Viet Nam. We have a duty, and I think the minister would recognize this, to ask what is his view as to developments. What are our reactions to the recently declared policy of the government of the United States in its desire to assist, by way of paramilitary power, the forces of the government of South Viet Nam? The committee will expect the minister to make a report on these three commissions because we are participating in them. We have many Canadians participating in the work of these commissions, in one way or another. We are spending considerable sums of money, and properly so, to help maintain these three commissions in an area of the world, so far removed. All of this indicates the interdependence of nations in this period in which we live, and the attendant responsibilities of peace loving countries like our own toward situations that exist in other parts of the world.

I believe every member of this house is extremely proud of the work that Canadians have been doing within recent years in southeast Asia. I believe there is no member of this house who would dare to vote against the request of the government for an additional $100,000 in the supplementary estimates in order to pay for our participation in the commission in Indochina. I am inclined to believe, Mr. Chairman, that if it had not been for these commissions in recent years, the history of this portion of the world would be entirely

different from what it now is. I believe they have a steadying and a pacifying influence in the area.
We are all aware of the fact that the commission is made up of representatives of one nation that is ordinarily labelled as being within the communist bloc, one western nation, namely our own, and another more or less neutral nation in the ideological warfare between the two major power blocs. I think Canadians ought to take a great deal of pride in what must be often a heartbreaking and frustrating task assigned to our people who are serving on the commission.
I am a little disturbed by the attitudes and even the activities of our good friend, neighbour and ally, the United States of America. I would hope that whereas we always welcome any advice that our good friend, neighbour and ally the United States decides it may wish to give us, that it may also be receptive to a bit of advice, on occasion at least, which we may give. I realize we are not a big nation like the United States, but I would hope they would be willing to lend an ear to expressions by the Canadian people. Most of us have been led to understand that an agreement, at least in principle, had been more or less arrived at between the warring factions in Viet Nam a considerable time ago. One cannot help, after reading the United Kingdom and Canadian press, but have the feeling that the United States of America is not, in spirit, really living up to the terms of that agreement in the policies that it is pursuing.
This is my whole plea. I feel that the Canadian government ought to use its good offices to appeal to the United States to do what it can to remove the appearance it has created, whether accidentally or by deliberate design, of preventing the implementation of the spirit of the agreement that has been recently concluded.
There seems to be a feeling that we can defeat the communists in Viet Nam by guerrilla counter attack. In this respect I would like to quote an article which appeared in last month's issue of the Atlantic Monthly entitled "The limits of defence." written by Arthur I. Waskow, who served as legislative assistant to a congressman from Wisconsin until a year ago. In analysing the situation, as printed at page 84 of the magazine, he says:
Successful guerrillas are not merely underground soldiers in an alien land. They need the support of the population and get it by demanding, or pretending to demand, social and economic reforms that would benefit the population around them. If the United States is prepared, with huge amounts of economic aid, to support social revolution even against western business and political associates in the local governments, it is not necessary to send commando fighters. If we refuse to support

basic social changes, sending commandos will not stop communist guerrillas, because our commandos will not get popular support.
The other attitude that seems to be adopted far too frequently in the western world is that we might be able to use the principle of a military deterrent in this part of Asia. On that Mr. Waskow has this to say, as recorded on page 85 of the magazine:
An attempt by the west to meet this dilemma by matching the Sino-Soviet alliance in sheer numbers of men under arms would be disastrous. The effect would be that of permanent limited wars, like those in Korea and Algeria, limited in the amount of violence allowable, so that no victory could be won, but seemingly unlimited in the length of time they might last. During these wars, the United States and France each experienced great pressures at home against keeping the war limited, and also great pressure against democratic civil liberties During the three short years of the Korean war, the United States had to deal with MacArthurism and McCarthyism. What would be the effect of 25 or 50 such years?
In the very short run, the balanced deterrent would undoubtedly be safer than a counterforce strategy, but it would only be useful as a way of getting the time to move to new solutions.
I would like to think that the Canadian government was doing its utmost to persuade our alies in Washington that a long term program or social change in southeast Asia is the only solution, and that guerrilla warfare and the deterrent of large numbers of armed personnel are not the long term answer, even though the deterrent may give us the time in which to work out the social changes needed.
I am not criticizing the attitude of the Canadian government in any way, shape or form. I believe we have been most useful in the past in this area of the world and, by the very nature of the request now before us, I know it is the intention of the government to continue to be a positive force in that area. I would only like to plead with our government to use its good offices to request a hearing in Washington with the end in view that we would not wind up with another Korea, Algeria or Congo situation in this part of the world.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The part which Canada has been and is playing in former Indo-China is a good example of the very large field we have in peace keeping activities, and this is one of the most useful types of work our nation can do. We are called on frequently for work of this type, and no country has a larger number of trained personnel in its departments of national defence or external affairs than Canada to undertake work of this kind.
I shall deal first with the situation in Laos. That can be divided into two different sectors. First of all there is the 14 nation conference which has been in session at Geneva for practically 10 months. When I say "14 26207-1-102i
Supply-External Affairs nations" I mean there are 13 national delegations there plus a triple delegation from Laos, one representing the group which is pro-western, one the group which is procommunist, and one representing Souvanna Phouma who is the head of the neutralist group in Laos. As I say, we have this threeheaded Laotian delegation in Geneva and by a process of patient negotiation, which has involved compromise on both sides, the representatives at Geneva have reached virtually complete agreement on arrangements to replace the 1954 general agreement for Laos.
While the issue is still in the balance it would not be helpful for me to attempt any detailed assessment of the results of their efforts, other than to say I think these results have been excellent, and they may well have set the standard for the disarmament negotiations which are to commence next week.
Canada's part of course has to do with the terms of reference for the international commission which will have to carry on in Laos after the conference in Geneva is ended. The primary role of our delegation has been to try to ensure that these terms of reference are such as to enable the commission to operate effectively in support of an internationally agreed settlement. However, an international agreement aimed at securing the independence, territorial integrity and neutrality of Laos presupposes an accepted and generally recognized government of Laos sharing these objectives and prepared to cooperate in bringing them about.
As hon. members know, each of these three factions in Laos is led by a prince, and the meetings which have taken place between the princes have not yet resulted in the formation of a government for Laos, although I am hopeful that result will be achieved fairly soon. Time, of course, does not seem to mean a great deal in the Orient. They have a meeting and then decide to adjourn for two or three weeks or a month, and then after much effort they meet again and the same process is repeated.
There has been some small narrowing of areas of disagreement, and Souvanna Phouma, who is the leader of the neutralist group, continues to show patience and perseverance in his efforts to complete the task of forming a unified government acceptable to all three parties. Mind you, until there is agreement on a government for Laos the conference in Geneva cannot complete its work. I think it would finish up very quickly once agreement had been reached on a government for this unhappy country.
Then I turn to Laos itself. There the international truce supervisory commission has been functioning as best it can. It has not been permitted to visit any of the scenes

Supply-External Affairs of real fighting, and no proper arrangements have been made for providing it with equipment under its own exclusive control, but I think the very fact that this commission is in Laos has greatly reduced the amount of fighting taking place, and I believe that if the commission had not been there there would have been a great deal more serious trouble than we have at the present time.
The head of the Canadian delegation is Leon Mayrand, who is our ambassador to Italy. He had done a splendid job; I do not think any Canadian could have done finer work than Mr. Mayrand has done. There has been fighting from time to time. There are protests made to the commission, sometimes protests from both sides, and then the fighting stops there and starts somewhere else. It goes on in this way, but nothing very serious has occurred as yet. I think that all the countries represented at the conference in Geneva on Laos really desire to see that country set up as a neutral state and to see the fighting stop. I think they all believe in the effectiveness of the international control commission, of which India is the chairman and Canada and Poland are the other two members. I cannot make any promises, because you never know what is going to happen-we learned that the hard way-but in any event there has been no starting of a third world war in Laos, and I think there is a reasonable chance that a settlement will be worked out. At the moment it all depends on these three princes.
With regard to Cambodia, this country is truly neutral and they have had very little trouble. The government of Cambodia is anxious that the truce commission should remain, otherwise I think-as the hon. member for Essex East said-that particular commission might well be disbanded, but we do not like to move to have it disbanded when the Cambodian government is anxious that it should remain. They express this desire from time to time, and I think Prince Sihanouk, who is the head of the government in Cambodia, has handled the affairs of that country extremely well. He attended at Geneva in May when the conference on Laos was opened, and he made the opening statement with what I thought was a very statesmanlike speech. He is a leader who is very well qualified and, as I have said, there is no really serious trouble in his country.
The situation in Viet Nam is a great deal more difficult. As hon. members know, in North Viet Nam and South Viet Nam the commission has jurisdiction over both separate countries. I think it would be unfair to single out the United States for blame in respect of the situation in South Viet Nam. The provocation, in my judgment, has come from North

Viet Nam. There have been troops infiltrating from North Viet Nam, and I am certain that the communists have been at the root of most of the trouble in South Viet Nam.
I agree with that.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There has been some very nasty guerrilla warfare going on there, with officials murdered, villagers blackmailed, villages destroyed, and all this sort of business, and the main blame for the trouble in South Viet Nam rests squarely on the shoulders of the communists-
I agree.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
-and not on the United States at all. Any action the United States has taken has been in a measure of defence against communist action. There the commission has many complaints from both sides. It does its best to examine these complaints. There is quite a long list of them now which have not yet been examined. I cannot say what will happen in South Viet Nam, or in North Viet Nam either for that matter, but here again Canada is playing her full part in restraining people and in trying to work out a solution to these internecine quarrels.
We have, of course, very many ways of discussing questions like this with the United States on a friendly basis, and questions such as Viet Nam are discussed practically daily with the state department. We will do what we can to urge moderation on everyone. Here again we will just have to hope that in the end a settlement can be worked out. It is not going to be easy; it may take a long time. I do not see any prospect of Canada being able to leave the Viet Nam commission at an early date, but as I said in opening, this is an area in which Canada is making a great contribution in the way of peace keeping activities and I think it is one of the finest contributions that has been made.
The hon. member for Essex East asked for the numbers of personnel involved. In Viet Nam there are four foreign service officers and eight on the administrative side, for a total of 12. In Laos there are three foreign service officers and three in administration, for a total of six. In Cambodia there are one foreign service officer and two on administration work, for a total of three. The military representation as of October 16 last is Viet Nam, 27 army officers, 26 other ranks, for a total of 53; two R.C.A.F. officers and two Royal Canadian Navy officers. In Laos there were 14 army officers and seven other ranks for a total of 21. Apparently there was also provision for one other officer and two other ranks in Cambodia, but these positions are not filled under present circumstances.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I may be allowed to make one further observation on what the minister has said, and to recall to him the attitude I took and the words I expressed when we discussed this matter in the house on September 11, 1961.
One appreciates, of course, that Canada as a member of these various commissions cannot on that account be expected to accept responsibility for solutions that rest with other powers. But we are on these commissions and we have an obligation to discharge. I know we are fulfilling that responsibility to the best of our competence and ability within the opportunities provided. It seems to me that we have the right to expect a more realistic appraisal of the consequences of the developments that are taking place not only in South Viet Nam but in Laos as well.
It is worth recalling that as late as 1956 the view was put forward that the policy of certain powers in the west toward Laos in particular was not a practical and wise policy, under the conditions that then prevailed. To have insisted upon a partisan government at that time was not a practical and wise policy. It is now agreed that there should be a government that is truly neutral.
I find it difficult to believe in the light of conditions that have prevailed since last January and in the light of the conflict among the three competing forces for government-the present royal government and the two other personalities involved, either in coalition or separately-that we can anticipate that there will be in fact a truly neutral government, because of aggressive intentions on the part of communist China in particular. We can only hope that a neutral government will result and that it will be able to work out conditions for the betterment of the people in that little Indo-China nation.
I believe we have the right to expect from our Secretary of State for External Affairs a wide appreciation of the situation as he sees it, not only in terms of the moment but as well of the future. If it is a fact that this is a theatre which might well occasion trouble extending far beyond south and southeast Asia, surely then this is a matter of great concern. The time for us to face the matter is now rather than wait until ominous events happen. We must at least try to anticipate what could happen, and discuss dispassionately and understanding^ what steps might be taken to avoid eventualities prejudicial to the maintenance of peace.
On September 11, 1961 the minister took issue with me when I said as reported at page 8185 of Hansard:
Supply-External Affairs
-it seems to me we ought to take a very realistic view of what is happening in the whole of Indo-China. While there may be a declaration of agreement on the question of the kind of neutrality that is to prevail regarding government in Laos, it would surprise me very much, in view of the record there and the infiltrations that are taking place via North Viet Nam and from across the Chinese-Burma border, if we can conclude that there have as yet been placed before us those guarantees which would give us the conviction that the solemn undertaking of those ideologically opposed to us will be observed. However, only time will tell.
The minister in commenting later, at page 8185 of Hansard, expressed the view that I was unduly pessimistic. Then he went on to express words of optimism which I do not believe were warranted at that time. I do not believe the minister on that occasion gave us justification for the optimism he expressed. I know the minister is optimistic by nature. Possibly he felt it would be better to create the impression that the situation was not a hopeless one by any means. There could be a very good argument for this attitude. As I see the situation, however, this is an area where the friction is of a character that must cause great concern not only to the minister and the government but to all of us.
Canada as a member of the commission will wish to be able to have an assessment made of her present and future role in a way that will warrant the belief that we have done everything we could to avoid any situation which the future might prove to be of the greatest concern. I am sure we are doing everything we can. But are we not entitled to an assessment from the minister as to what lies ahead? Will there be a truly neutral government, or will it be a tool of aggressive powers that intend to violate the peace of the area? What are the implications of this for us? What is the attitude of the present government toward the operation of the commission? Is the commission able to fulfil its functions? Is it able to accomplish the mandate given to it? If not, why not? Are there obstacles still being placed in its way as was the situation last September when, as the minister indicated, necessary military equipment was not made available?
The situation with regard to Viet Nam is no less difficult. It is much more serious. What is the attitude of the government of South Viet Nam to the commission? As a member of the commission do we have access and has the commission access to the territory in North Viet Nam? Do we have contact with the governing bodies in North Viet Nam? The minister said our role would be to do all we could to provide a balance between the discordant elements. I am sure the minister was sincere when he said that. I am sure Canada

Supply-External Affairs does take that position. I merely ask whether the opportunities are present for us to be able to exercise on all sides the influence implied in the minister's assurance that we would do everything we could to pacify the competing forces.
These are some of the questions in the minds of all of us as we read from day to day of the continuous conflict, a conflict that is being assisted by outside participation, providing thereby for a situation which I think demands on the part of the minister the frankest possible statement that he feels he can make in respect of situations which we are led ot believe and which our own judgment suggests are calculated to bring about serious and dangerous provocations for widening conflict.
We in the west have often been accused of not facing situations, of always being behind events. Here is one situation that threatens. What can we do about it? What are we doing about it? What assessment is made of the situation by countries with which we have a close interest in the western world? This is the kind of comment I think we should like to receive from the minister today. We assume that Canada cannot rectify this question by herself. All the good will in the world on the part of the minister cannot rectify this situation. However, we are on these commissions. We are in this turbulent area where vigorous guerrilla warfare is now being carried on. It is a form of warfare which is intended to arrest the infiltration from the north into South Viet Nam. We shall not avoid these problems by refusing to face their consequences.
I am asking the minister now if he does not think that the seriousness of the situation -it is one which I thought was serious last summer, and it continues to be even more serious-is one that demands from the minister a more penetrating analysis, I was going to say, or a more penetrating report on the situation as he sees it. I think that is something which we are entitled to ask. Other governments have felt that it was their duty to give a much more detailed reply on events as they saw them than we have received today. These other nations may have a heavier responsibility. However, as the minister has often stated, although a smaller power our opportunity is not necessarily less on that account. That being the case, I think the minister possibly could give us a more definitive appreciation of the situation.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am very grateful to the hon. member for inviting me to enter into the field of prophecy. However, I am neither a prophet nor the son of a prophet. I find that it does not pay very big dividends to start prophesying when one is head of the Department of

External Affairs. What does pay dividends is not taking an attitude that any situation is hopeless. If the foreign minister adopted that attitude, it would be much better if he were in the Senate or somewhere else instead of being in this office. After all, there are serious situations in many parts of the world. Canada is involved in as many of them as any other middle power, and is playing a part which is as big as or bigger than the part played by any other middle power in these various areas.
What will happen in Indo-China in the final analysis will depend upon what red China decides to do, possibly on what the United States decides to do, and possibly on what some other large countries decide to do. However, we are able to exercise a good deal of influence on all these countries. From my experience at the Geneva conference on Laos I would say that no country represented there wants a world war started over Laos. I shall be greatly surprised if, with regard to Viet Nam, there is not exactly the same reaction. There may be all kinds of guerrilla warfare and troubles of one kind and another; however, I do not think red China wants a war started over any part of IndoChina.
So far as the western countries are concerned, there is in existence the SEATO pact. We are not a member of SEATO; however, I think the leaders of these other countries realize that it would be insanity to have a nuclear war break out as a result of anything happening in Indo-China. This is the main reason that I do not adopt the attitude that the situation there cannot be solved. My experience is that all the countries sitting in on the conference on Laos at Geneva desire to have that country really neutral and that they desire to have a condition in which a truce commission can function properly.
I would be the last one to assert that there are not many frustrating events happening in the work of the two commissions. I refer to the one in Laos and also the one in Viet Nam. We are not able to do all the things we should like to do. For one thing, there is a division on the commissions. The Poles are there representing the communist world, and often it just is not a situation where you can get agreement. Sometimes decisions are made on a majority basis. However, by and large, I think Canada's part in all three of these countries in former Indo-China has been very much worth while.

The minister did not answer some of the questions that were addressed to him by my friend the hon. member for Essex East, as I understand them, about the powers and responsibilities of the commission, and the opportunity to discharge those

responsibilities, particularly in Viet Nam; whether they had had access to the northern or the communist part and, if so, whether they had had any opportunity, because of that access, to examine what was going on there. After all, these commissions were set up in conditions which were much different from those which exist now. They were set up to police a cease fire. However, they have taken on responsibilities-and I am certainly not complaining about this matter- which were never entertained when they were established.
I think they have discharged those responsibilities to the best of their ability, having regard to the fact that there is a communist, a non-communist and an anti-communist on each commission. Certainly the Canadian members of the commissions have discharged their share of the responsibilities in a manner that has done great credit to themselves and indeed to our country. Hence it is not a question of complaining about the work of the commission; it is a question of trying to find out whether, in new situations, these commissions, especially those in Viet Nam and Laos, which are the two that matter, have now an opportunity to do the job which is required in these new situations, or whether in fact these commissions can be used as a front behind which forces are at work which will not make for neutral countries in that area but for something much more dangerous. I am thinking of communist governments in these countries, especially in Laos, where the communist infiltration has gone very far indeed, backed by communist forces outside of Laos; forces now getting across the border into Cambodia. We know, of course, what the situation is in Viet Nam. It is a situation which is bound to arouse anxiety.
I think it is perfectly in order for us, without asking the minister to prophesy what is going to happen in the future, to find out whether the commissions can in fact do the job which they are required to do in these circumstances. The minister said that he does not intend to be a prophet. I think he is very wise in not attempting to be a prophet. However, the minister very often- and he is not being criticized for this fact- has prophesied optimistically about what would happen in respect of this situation. We hope his optimism will be justified. He was optimistic about the situation in Laos, Viet Nam and Cambodia when we last debated this subject. But that situation certainly has not improved. I hope it has not deteriorated to a point where it can become a real danger to peace in the world.
The minister said that what optimism he has is based on the fact that as a result of his experience at the conference at Geneva
Supply-External Affairs it is his opinion that all members of that conference-I hope I am not misquoting him, because I am certainly paraphrasing-sincerely desired a neutral Laos, a neutral Cambodia and presumably a neutral Viet Nam; that they are countries which could be isolated and insulated from the cold war.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did not say anything about a neutral Viet Nam.

Well, a neutral Laos and a neutral Cambodia. But it is hard for me to believe that the Chinese communist representative at this meeting was really anxious or even willing to have a neutral Laos. If that were the case, it is hard to understand the support that the Chinese communist government is giving to the Pathet Lao forces which, as I see it, are trying to prevent a neutral Laos and trying to set up in that country a communist state or a state which will be allied to the Chinese communist empire.
Similarly in Viet Nam, as the minister has said-and it has been said by others-the force mainly responsible for the civil war, because it is civil war, is the intervention of Chinese communism in that area. That is the main force behind the intervention that is causing the trouble. I am sure that is true. You have the Chinese communists supporting one faction in Laos. You have the Chinese communists supporting the communist side in North Viet Nam. You have these North Viet Nam forces now facing South Viet Nam which has been very actively, and understandably in view of the situation, supported by the United States of America.
It may well be, I am sure it is the case, that no one at the Geneva conference and perhaps no one in this area of the world wants a world war to start over Laos or Viet Nam, any more than people wanted world war II to start over Danzig. But you have a situation now where you have two parties to the cold war, the Chinese communist empire and the United States, facing each other, one in South Viet Nam and the other in North Viet Nam. That is a danger to peace. Perhaps no one wants this situation to develop into a world war, but on the other hand perhaps the Chinese communist regime wants a united communist Viet Nam. It is certainly operating for that purpose.
To what extent then are the forces on the southern side in South Viet Nam, willing to fight to resist that kind of penetration. In that fight what is the nature and extent of the United States intervention going to be? I read the other day-this has been stated in Washington and I do not think it is any secret, because the United States has given a great deal of information recently about its activities

Supply-External Affairs in Viet Nam-that there are about 4,500 United States troops operating there. Ostensibly they are there to train and help to equip the South Viet Nam forces who are defending their country against civil invasion from the north. But training intervention of this kind is gradually shifting to more active intervention in operations. Surely this is a dangerous position. I do not know whether greater danger can be avoided; I hope it can.
I am not at the moment criticizing the United States for the shifting nature of its intervention. This may well be required unless the United States is willing to abandon its friend, President Diem, and the government of South Viet Nam. In that regard however, our anxiety is increased by the fact that the popular base of support for the government of South Viet Nam is not very deep or broad. At least there have been indications recently that the position of the government there, which the United States and other western powers are backing, is pretty shaky. How far then will western intervention go to preserve this government because it is the friendly government of South Viet Nam and is opposed to the communist government in the north?
All these questions are of very great importance. They would be important to Canada whether or not we were represented on the commission; just as what happened in Danzig in 1939 was important to Canada, and what happened at Sarajevo in 1914 was important to Canada. But we have an additional responsibility because we have accepted, and we have rightly accepted membership on these commissions, and we have discharged our responsibility on them in a way that has brought credit to the men on these commissions and to the government and people of Canada.
I wonder, therefore, whether the minister can give us some further information especially about the work of the commission in Viet Nam. To what extent is the commission consulted in respect of relations between the government of the United States, the government of South Viet Nam and, if there is any relationship, with the government of the north, or is it being used as a screen behind which dangerous forces are at work? In the future it might even be asked to accept some responsibility for developments there without in fact having any power or opportunity to control in any way those developments. As Canada is represented on these commissions, I think we are justified in expressing some preoccupation with this matter and in asking for this kind of information if the minister feels it can be given.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the commission visits Hanoi in North Viet Nam from time


to time. I have had no reports of their interviewing Ho-Chi-Minh, the president of North Viet Nam, this year. Mind you, their ability to get around and check the whole situation is comparatively limited. I do not think the commission can be attacked fairly on the ground that it is simply being used for someone to build up trouble behind it. If that were a proper criticism, then one would perhaps be justified in asking that the commission be withdrawn.
I do not think that is the case. They do what they can to check these incidents. One incident, for example, involved the murder of a South Viet Nam military officer who was attached to the commission. He was murdered in a most cold blooded way, and the commission has had the greatest difficulty in finding out the facts behind the murder. They have also had great difficulty in getting the facts with regard to various other incidents that have taken place.
It would be unfair to make the commission assume responsibility for all that goes on in Viet Nam. When the Leader of the Opposition referred to the red Chinese coming into South Viet Nam, I think he was wrong. The infiltration is from North Viet Nam and not, as far as I am aware, by red Chinese troops either in South Viet Nam or in Laos. By the very nature of the operation of the commission its work cannot be perfect. Those Canadians who are serving on the commission simply do the best they can under conditions which are extremely trying.
Looking at the broad picture, I think the presence of these commissions in the area has prevented a big war breaking out. I may be wrong in that view. As the Leader of the Opposition knows, it is quite impossible for anyone to be certain just what would have happened had the commissions not been there, but I think they are a restraining influence. It must never be forgotten that the commissions themselves are divided. It is not as though they go in as a team of three working together. That is not the case at all. They go in with the representative of one country working very closely with the communists, and it is a very difficult situation.

I did not mean to give the impression, perhaps I did give it that red Chinese troops as such had moved across the border. I have no reason to believe that, and no evidence I have seen would support that. But there is no doubt that the communists from the north have red Chinese forces behind them, that these communists from North Viet Nam who are doing the infiltrating are in very close relationship to the Chinese communist government. This is how it is being done. I am glad to hear the

minister say that the commissions have been a restraining influence. I am sure that is right. It has been a good thing to have them there. The time is going to come when perhaps their usefulness is over, in which case they should be withdrawn. I believe the government has considered withdrawing the commissions from Cambodia and Laos, but perhaps it has been a good thing to have them there in view of events in the last year or two.
It is useful to have the minister's opinion that the commissions are not being used as a screen behind which activities could be carried on of which we would not approve. The danger remains, however and I am sure the minister will agree with me, that behind the North Vietnamese are the Chinese communists who have not interfered openly as yet any more than they interfered openly in North Korea in the early days of the war there. Behind the South Vietnamese are the United States forces. If this civil war can be confined to the forces of Viet Nam, on one side or the other, perhaps there is not going to be any widespread trouble. But if, in fact, the war broadens out to the point where those who are helping each side get in conflict with each other, then anything can happen.
The other day when it was announced the United States had sent some more troops into Viet Nam, a great deal of publicity was given to this. The minister will recall a statement was issued from Peking that if this kind of thing continued the Chinese government will consider what kind of action it will have to take to support its friends. This is what happened in Korea. At the beginning there was no Chinese intervention. It was felt by a lot of people that there would be no Chinese intervention, but the Chinese government said that under certain circumstances they would intervene and they did intervene. We missed world war III by a hair's breadth. Let us hope that does not happen in Viet Nam.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I should point out that there are no United States combat troops in South Viet Nam.

I think there are United States combat troops there for training purposes. There are 4,500 according to the announcement from Washington, and they are there to help train the Viet Nam forces to meet the forces from the north.

I believe that the vast majority of the Canadian people will always be grateful that our Secretary of State for External Affairs likes to regard himself as an optimist. I would hate to think of the attitude of the
Supply-External Affairs Canadian government towards the world scene if our Secretary of State for External Affairs were anything else but an optimist.
There has been a bit of discussion of the role and duties of the commission in that part of the world. I had never expected that the role of the commission would be to ensure that that part of the world would some day be in either the communist or the western camp. I had always imagined that the role of this commission was primarily to maintain peace and to prevent an outbreak of war, to limit any violence or to attempt to use its influence to keep violence to the lowest possible level.
Then, my basic reason for rising was that I did want to make it perfectly clear that it is our contention that the basic cause of unrest is that the people in the area of the world now know that the conditions of life which they have experienced in the past can be improved upon. There has to be a change in the social and economic lives of the people in that area. I agree with the minister when he contends that the communists are the immediate cause of the disturbances. They will always exploit to the utmost, on behalf of their ideology, any social or economic complaints of the people anywhere in the world. Our only plea was that our reply to the challenge of the communists, especially the reply of the United States, ought to be directed towards removing the economic and social complaints of the people in order to take away from the communists their most valuable source of ammunition.
Before I sit down, however, I should like to ask the minister a specific question. Has any report ever been issued to the government as to why a Canadian official was murdered in that area? The minister referred to this only a few minutes ago. I should like also to ask him another question. Have any Canadians, either from the Department of External Affairs or the Department of National Defence, been sent home for reasons other than the normal reasons of leave, furlough, et cetera? If so, for what reason were they sent to Canada?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I was referring to the murder of a South Vietnamese colonel, not a Canadian. I believe there was a Canadian murdered some years before I took over the portfolio.

It was one of our
own.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, there was a Canadian murdered that time. I have no report on that particular incident. From time to time, Canadians are brought home, but I think it would be of no benefit for me to go into that any further.

minister if he can enlighten us as to whether the small Christian colony in or near Hanoi, where Canadians used to foregather quite frequently, has been permitted to continue, or have the personnel left?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have no knowledge of that, but I shall be glad to get the information and send it to the hon. member.

The minister seemed to be hesitant in replying to the latter part of my question. To the best of his knowledge, have any Canadians been sent home, other than in normal circumstances, and have they been found guilty of violating the laws of our country?

speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman.

I wonder whether or not the minister would care to tell us about that? I believe that Canadians realize we are not without sin and that we sometimes err. I feel that the committee is entitled to know what has happened.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the situation is this: While it would be very nice from a curiosity point of view to make statements on facts like this, unfortunately the matter very seriously affects those Canadians still serving in Indo-China and for that reason I do not think it is in the public interest that I should go any further.

Mexico is a member of the organization of American states. It may be that many citizens in that great and friendly country would regard, as one of the most effective ways for Canada to observe the sesquicentennial anniversary of the independence of the republic of Mexico, a clarification of the government's intentions with regard to joining the organization of American states.
I do not say that everyone in Mexico would accept that as the proper way for Canada to pay tribute to Mexico, but I suspect that the encouragement given by the minister himself on his peregrinations to Mexico as well as to other Latin American countries, and by the Prime Minister, has whetted the appetite of many people as to Canada's intentions.

It will 'be recalled that the minister himself took the initiative in saying that the government was giving careful attention to membership in the organization of American states; and indeed the Prime Minister, on the occasion of his official visit to Mexico, by the emphasis he gave to the matter at any rate seemed to have gone a step further.
